theory.intro: If $P(x)=(x-\alpha)^{m}Q(x)$ with $m>1$ and $Q(\alpha)\ne0$, then $\alpha$ has exact multiplicity $m$. The product rule gives $P'(x)=(x-\alpha)^{m-1}\left[mQ(x)+(x-\alpha)Q'(x)\right]$. At $x=\alpha$, the bracket equals $mQ(\alpha)\ne0$, so $\alpha$ is a zero of multiplicity exactly $m-1$ of $P'$. Differentiating therefore counts how many times a zero repeats.
facts: If $P(\alpha)=0$ but $P'(\alpha)\ne0$, then $\alpha$ is a zero of multiplicity $1$.
If $P(\alpha)=0$ and $P'(\alpha)=0$, then $(x-\alpha)^{2}$ is a factor of $P(x)$.
If $P(\alpha)$, $P'(\alpha)$ and $P''(\alpha)$ are all zero, then $(x-\alpha)^{3}$ is a factor of $P(x)$.
In general $\alpha$ has multiplicity $m$ when $P(\alpha)=P'(\alpha)=\cdots=P^{(m-1)}(\alpha)=0$ and $P^{(m)}(\alpha)\ne0$.
A zero of $P'(x)$ is a repeated zero of $P(x)$ only if it is also a zero of $P(x)$.
A stationary point of $P$ that lies on the $x$-axis is always a repeated zero of $P$.
steps: Keep differentiating until a derivative is not zero at $x=\alpha$.
State the multiplicity as the order of the first non-zero derivative.

workedExamples.question_text:
Use derivatives to determine the multiplicity of the stated zero in each polynomial.
(a) $P(x)=x^{2}-7x+10$, at $x=2$.
(b) $Q(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$, at $x=1$.
(c) $R(x)=x^{3}+6x^{2}+12x+8$, at $x=-2$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{aligned}P(2)&=4-14+10=0\\P'(x)&=2x-7\\P'(2)&=-3\ne0\end{aligned}$
The zero $2$ has multiplicity $1$.

(b) $\begin{aligned}Q(1)&=1-3+2=0\\Q'(x)&=3x^{2}-3\\Q'(1)&=0\\Q''(x)&=6x\\Q''(1)&=6\ne0\end{aligned}$
The first non-zero derivative at $x=1$ is $Q''$, so the multiplicity is $2$.

(c) $\begin{aligned}R(-2)&=-8+24-24+8=0\\R'(x)&=3x^{2}+12x+12\\R'(-2)&=12-24+12=0\\R''(x)&=6x+12\\R''(-2)&=0\\R'''(x)&=6\\R'''(-2)&=6\ne0\end{aligned}$
The first non-zero derivative at $x=-2$ is $R'''$, so the multiplicity is $3$.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) A polynomial satisfies $P(-5)=P'(-5)=0$ and $P''(-5)\ne0$. Find the highest power of $(x+5)$ that divides $P(x)$.
(b) A monic quartic $Q(x)$ satisfies $Q(4)=Q'(4)=Q''(4)=0$, $Q'''(4)\ne0$ and $Q(-2)=0$. Write $Q(x)$ in factored form.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The first non-zero derivative at $x=-5$ is $P''$, so the multiplicity is exactly $2$. The highest power is $(x+5)^{2}$.

(b) The derivative conditions give a zero of multiplicity $3$ at $x=4$. The zero $-2$ supplies another linear factor. These account for all four factors, and the leading coefficient is $1$.
$Q(x)=(x-4)^{3}(x+2)$

workedExamples.question_text: Let $P(x)=(x-2)^{3}Q(x)$, where $Q(2)\ne0$. State which of $P(2)$, $P'(2)$, $P''(2)$ and $P'''(2)$ are zero.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Since $Q(2)\ne0$, the zero $2$ has exact multiplicity $3$.
$\begin{aligned}P(2)&=0\\P'(2)&=0\\P''(2)&=0\\P'''(2)&\ne0\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-75x+250$ has a double zero. Find the zeroes of $P'(x)$ and identify the double zero of $P(x)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$P'(x)=3x^{2}-75$
Solving $P'(x)=0$,
$\begin{aligned}3x^{2}-75&=0\\x^{2}&=25\\x&=\pm5\end{aligned}$
Test both candidates in $P$.
$\begin{aligned}P(5)&=125-375+250=0\\P(-5)&=-125+375+250=500\end{aligned}$
Only $5$ is a zero of both $P$ and $P'$. Also, $P''(5)=6(5)=30\ne0$, so $5$ is the double zero.

workedExamples.question_text: The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+k$ has a double zero. Find the two possible values of $k$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}P'(x)&=3x^{2}-12x\\&=3x(x-4)\end{aligned}$
A double zero must satisfy both $P'(x)=0$ and $P(x)=0$. The candidates are $x=0$ and $x=4$.
For $x=0$,
$\begin{aligned}P(0)&=k=0\\k&=0\end{aligned}$
For $x=4$,
$\begin{aligned}P(4)&=64-96+k=0\\k&=32\end{aligned}$
Since $P''(x)=6x-12$ is non-zero at both candidates, each gives exact multiplicity $2$. The possible values are $k=0$ and $k=32$.

workedExamples.question_text: The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}+bx^{2}+cx-4$ has a double zero at $x=2$. Find $b$ and $c$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use $P(2)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}8+4b+2c-4&=0\\2b+c&=-2\end{aligned}$
Since $P'(x)=3x^{2}+2bx+c$, use $P'(2)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}12+4b+c&=0\\4b+c&=-12\end{aligned}$
Subtract the first equation from the second.
$\begin{aligned}2b&=-10\\b&=-5\\c&=-2-2(-5)\\&=8\end{aligned}$
Thus $b=-5$ and $c=8$. With these values, $P''(2)=12-10=2\ne0$, confirming a double zero.

workedExamples.question_text: The polynomial $P(x)=ax^{3}+bx+c$ has a double zero at $x=-1$. It leaves a remainder of $16$ when divided by $x-3$. Find $a$, $b$ and $c$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The double zero gives $P'(-1)=0$ and $P(-1)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}P'(x)&=3ax^{2}+b\\3a+b&=0\\b&=-3a\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}-a-b+c&=0\\-a+3a+c&=0\\c&=-2a\end{aligned}$
By the remainder theorem, $P(3)=16$.
$\begin{aligned}27a+3b+c&=16\\27a-9a-2a&=16\\16a&=16\\a&=1\\b&=-3\\c&=-2\end{aligned}$
With these values, $P(-1)=P'(-1)=0$ and $P''(-1)=-6\ne0$, confirming a double zero. Also, $P(3)=27-9-2=16$.

workedExamples.question_text: Let $P(x)=ux^{3}+vx^{2}+wx+z$, where $u\ne0$. Show that if $P$ has a triple zero, it occurs at $x=-\dfrac{v}{3u}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let the triple zero be $\alpha$. Then $P''(\alpha)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}P'(x)&=3ux^{2}+2vx+w\\P''(x)&=6ux+2v\\6u\alpha+2v&=0\\\alpha&=-\dfrac{v}{3u}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: The equation $ux^{3}+vx^{2}+w=0$, where $u$, $v$ and $w$ are non-zero, has a double root. Show that the root is $x=-\dfrac{2v}{3u}$ and that $27u^{2}w+4v^{3}=0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let $P(x)=ux^{3}+vx^{2}+w$.
$\begin{aligned}P'(x)&=3ux^{2}+2vx\\&=x(3ux+2v)\end{aligned}$
The candidates are $x=0$ and $x=-\dfrac{2v}{3u}$. Since $P(0)=w\ne0$, the double root is $x=-\dfrac{2v}{3u}$.
Substitute this root into $P(x)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}u\left(-\dfrac{2v}{3u}\right)^{3}+v\left(-\dfrac{2v}{3u}\right)^{2}+w&=0\\-\dfrac{8v^{3}}{27u^{2}}+\dfrac{4v^{3}}{9u^{2}}+w&=0\\\dfrac{4v^{3}}{27u^{2}}+w&=0\\4v^{3}+27u^{2}w&=0\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}+rx+s$, where $r\ne0$, has a double zero. Show that $4r^{3}+27s^{2}=0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let the double zero be $\alpha$. Use $P'(\alpha)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}P'(x)&=3x^{2}+r\\3\alpha^{2}+r&=0\\\alpha^{2}&=-\dfrac{r}{3}\end{aligned}$
Use $P(\alpha)=0$.
$\begin{aligned}\alpha^{3}+r\alpha+s&=0\\\alpha(\alpha^{2}+r)&=-s\\\alpha\left(-\dfrac{r}{3}+r\right)&=-s\\\dfrac{2r\alpha}{3}&=-s\\\alpha&=-\dfrac{3s}{2r}\end{aligned}$
Substitute into $\alpha^{2}=-\dfrac{r}{3}$.
$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{9s^{2}}{4r^{2}}&=-\dfrac{r}{3}\\27s^{2}&=-4r^{3}\\4r^{3}+27s^{2}&=0\end{aligned}$

foundation.question_text:
It is known that $x=5$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{2}-10x+25$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.
foundation.solution_text:
$P(5)=25-50+25$
$=0$
$P'(x)=2x-10$
$P'(5)=10-10$
$=0$
$P''(x)=2$
$P''(5)=2$
The first derivative that is not zero at $x=5$ is $P''$, so $5$ is a zero of multiplicity $2$.

foundation.question_text:
It is known that $x=4$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{2}-9x+20$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.

It is known that $x=4$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{3}-12x^{2}+48x-64$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.

It is known that $x=2$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{3}-5x^{2}+8x-4$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.
foundation.solution_text:
$P(2)=8-20+16-4$
$=0$
$P'(x)=3x^{2}-10x+8$
$P'(2)=12-20+8$
$=0$
$P''(x)=6x-10$
$P''(2)=12-10$
$=2$
The first derivative that is not zero at $x=2$ is $P''$, so $2$ is a zero of multiplicity $2$.

foundation.question_text:
A polynomial $P(x)$ satisfies $P(6)=0$, $P'(6)=0$ and $P''(6)\ne0$.
Write down the highest power of $(x-6)$ that is a factor of $P(x)$.
foundation.solution_text:
$P(6)=0$ and $P'(6)=0$, so $(x-6)^{2}$ is a factor.
$P''(6)\ne0$, so $(x-6)^{3}$ is not a factor.
The highest power is $(x-6)^{2}$.

foundation.question_text:
$P(x)=(x+4)^{3}Q(x)$, where $Q(-4)\ne0$.
State which of $P(-4)$, $P'(-4)$, $P''(-4)$ and $P'''(-4)$ are zero.

It is known that $x=-2$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{2}+4x+4$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.
foundation.solution_text:
$P(-2)=4-8+4$
$=0$
$P'(x)=2x+4$
$P'(-2)=-4+4$
$=0$
$P''(x)=2$
$P''(-2)=2$
The first derivative that is not zero at $x=-2$ is $P''$, so $-2$ is a zero of multiplicity $2$.

foundation.question_text:
It is known that $x=-1$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.

development.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-12x+16$ has a double zero.
Find the zeroes of $P'(x)$ and determine which one is the double zero of $P(x)$.

The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+k$ has a double zero.
Find the two possible values of $k$.
development.solution_text:
$P'(x)=3x^{2}-18x$
$=3x(x-6)$
$P'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=6$.
A double zero must satisfy $P(x)=0$ as well.
$P(0)=k$
$k=0$
$P(6)=216-324+k$
$=k-108$
$k=108$
The two possible values are $k=0$ and $k=108$.

development.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}+bx^{2}+cx-9$ has a double zero at $x=3$.
Find $b$ and $c$.

It is known that $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$ is a zero of $P(x)=9x^{3}+12x^{2}-11x+2$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.
development.solution_text:
$P\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{4}{3}-\dfrac{11}{3}+2$
$=-2+2$
$=0$
$P'(x)=27x^{2}+24x-11$
$P'\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=3+8-11$
$=0$
$P''(x)=54x+24$
$P''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=18+24$
$=42$
The first derivative that is not zero at $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$ is $P''$, so $\dfrac{1}{3}$ is a zero of multiplicity $2$.

development.question_text: Show that $x=2$ is a double root of the equation $x^{4}-4x^{3}+5x^{2}-4x+4=0$.

It is known that $x=2$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{4}-4x^{3}+16x-16$.
Use derivatives to find its multiplicity.

A monic polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $4$ satisfies $P(2)=P'(2)=P''(2)=0$, $P'''(2)\ne0$ and $P(-1)=0$.
Write $P(x)$ in factored form.
development.solution_text:
$P(2)=P'(2)=P''(2)=0$ and $P'''(2)\ne0$, so $x=2$ is a zero of multiplicity $3$.
$P(-1)=0$, so $x=-1$ is also a zero.
The multiplicities $3$ and $1$ add to the degree $4$, so there are no other zeroes.
$P(x)=(x-2)^{3}(x+1)$

mastery.question_text: Show that if $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$ has a triple root, then that root is $x=-\dfrac{b}{3a}$.
mastery.solution_text:
Let the triple root be $x=\alpha$, so $P(\alpha)=P'(\alpha)=P''(\alpha)=0$.
$P(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$
$P'(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c$
$P''(x)=6ax+2b$
$P''(\alpha)=6a\alpha+2b$
$=0$
$\alpha=-\dfrac{b}{3a}$

mastery.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=ax^{3}+bx+c$ has a double zero at $x=-2$, and leaves a remainder of $-27$ when divided by $x-1$.
Find $a$, $b$ and $c$.

The equation $Ax^{3}+Bx^{2}+D=0$, where $A$, $B$ and $D$ are non-zero, has a double root.
Show that the double root is $x=-\dfrac{2B}{3A}$, and hence that $27A^{2}D+4B^{3}=0$.
mastery.solution_text:
$P(x)=Ax^{3}+Bx^{2}+D$
$P'(x)=3Ax^{2}+2Bx$
$=x(3Ax+2B)$
$P'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=-\dfrac{2B}{3A}$.
$P(0)=D$, and $D\ne0$, so $x=0$ is not a zero of $P(x)$.
The double root is therefore $x=-\dfrac{2B}{3A}$.
$A\left(-\dfrac{2B}{3A}\right)^{3}+B\left(-\dfrac{2B}{3A}\right)^{2}+D=0$
$-\dfrac{8B^{3}}{27A^{2}}+\dfrac{4B^{3}}{9A^{2}}+D=0$
$\dfrac{4B^{3}}{27A^{2}}+D=0$
$4B^{3}+27A^{2}D=0$
